files.lesson.md: --- order: 13 unit: reals9 node: AC9M9N01 n4 uses: [AC9M9N01 n2] assumes: [AC9M8N01 n1, AC9M8N01 n2] connection: pizza-value title: Formulas with π and roots summary: "Put real numbers into a formula and keep π or the root exact until the end. Often the π cancels when you compare, so you never need its digits." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A large pizza or two medium ones: which is more pizza? Your answer depends on a number that never ends." --- Formulas for circles and diagonals have π and square roots in them. You can keep them exact, round at the end, or sometimes skip the digits altogether. ## Predict: one large or two mediums ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing before calculating shows who thinks area doubles with width (so one 30 cm is more than two 23 cm) rather than with the square of the radius." check: type: predict q: "A shop sells a large pizza that's 30 cm across and a medium that's 23 cm across. Is one large pizza more pizza than two mediums?" options: - "No: two mediums are more pizza" - "Yes: one large is more pizza" - "They're about the same" - "You can't tell without the price" actual: "No: two mediums are more. The large has area π × 15² = 225π ≈ 707 cm². A medium has π × 11.5² = 132.25π, so two have 264.5π ≈ 831 cm²." ``` The sizes are made up for the task. Don't use a calculator yet: is one large more than two mediums? ## Run: calculate it ```step stage: run insight: "A calculator's π key keeps many digits, so the area of the large pizza comes out close to its exact value of 225π." check: { type: number, q: "Use your calculator's π key. What's the area of the large pizza, $\\pi \\times 15^2$, to the nearest whole number of cm²? Was your prediction right?", answer: 707, tolerance: 0.6, explain: "π × 225 = 706.86…, so 707 cm²." } ``` Now work out the medium's area, $\pi \times 11.5^2$, and double it. ## Investigate: π stays exact ```step stage: investigate insight: "Write areas as a number times π and compare the numbers: the π is the same on both sides. Pia rounds π to 3 and calls the result exact." tasks: - check: type: question q: "What's the exact area of a circle of radius 5 cm?" options: ["$25\\pi$ cm²", "$78.5$ cm²", "$10\\pi$ cm²", "$25$ cm²"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "78.5 is rounded: π was cut to 3.14.", "Radius squared, not doubled: 5² = 25.", "Don't forget π."] explain: "A = πr² = π × 25 = 25π cm²." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#pia" text: "Pia finds the large pizza's area. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: round-early explain: "Line 4: with π = 3 the area is only approximate. The exact area is 225π cm², about 707 cm²." - check: type: number q: "A pizza of radius 15 cm has area $225\\pi$. Two mediums have area $264.5\\pi$ in total. Which has the bigger number in front of π? Type that number." answer: 264.5 explain: "264.5 is bigger than 225, so two mediums are more pizza. The π is the same on both sides, so it doesn't matter what its digits are." ``` ### Keep it exact Here's the comparison without ever using π's digits. ```worked r = 15 :: Large: half of 30. A = \pi \times 15^2 = 225\pi :: Keep π. r = 11.5 :: Medium: half of 23. A = \pi \times 11.5^2 = 132.25\pi :: One medium. 2 \times 132.25\pi = 264.5\pi :: Two mediums. 264.5 > 225 :: The π is on both sides: compare the numbers. ``` Now try one on paper: one circle of radius 6 cm or two of radius 4 cm. Which is bigger, and by how many π? Type the difference in π units (a number). ### Find the mistake Read Pia's working. Is 675 exact? ### The bigger number ## Modify: change the shapes ```step stage: modify insight: "Changing the formula: a calculator answer to one decimal place, the diameter given instead of the radius, and two roots multiplied exactly." tasks: - hint: ["π × 10² = π × 100.", "Use the π key."] check: { type: number, q: "A circle has radius 10 cm. What's its area to 1 decimal place?", answer: 314.2, tolerance: 0.06, explain: "π × 100 = 314.159…, so 314.2 cm²." } smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Just the square: what's $10^2$?", answer: 100, explain: "10 × 10 = 100." } - hint: ["Halve the diameter first.", "Radius 6, then square."] check: { type: number, q: "A circle has diameter 12 cm. Its exact area is $k\\pi$ cm². What's $k$?", answer: 36, explain: "r = 6 and 6² = 36: 36π." } - hint: ["√2 × √8 = √16.", "√16 is a whole number."] check: { type: number, q: "Edge case: what is $\\sqrt{2} \\times \\sqrt{8}$ exactly?", answer: 4, explain: "√2 × √8 = √16 = 4: the roots multiply into a whole number." } ``` ### Area to 1 decimal place ### Diameter given ### Two roots ## Practise: exact and rounded ```step stage: practise insight: "Using formulas with π and roots, exact and rounded, mixed; the review keeps ranges fresh." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A circle has radius 4 cm. Its exact area is $k\\pi$ cm². What's $k$?" answer: 16 explain: "4² = 16: 16π." - check: type: number q: "Use the π key: the area of a circle of radius 7 cm, to 1 decimal place." answer: 153.9 tolerance: 0.06 explain: "π × 49 = 153.938…, so 153.9 cm²." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Just the square: what's $7^2$?", answer: 49, explain: "7 × 7 = 49." } - check: type: number q: "A square has side 3 cm. Its diagonal is $\\sqrt{18}$ cm. To 2 decimal places, how long is it?" answer: 4.24 tolerance: 0.006 explain: "√18 = 4.2426…, so 4.24." - check: type: question q: "Review: a hole passes if $19.95 \\le x \\le 20.05$. Does 20.05 pass?" options: ["Yes: ≤ keeps the end", "No: it's on the end"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "≤ means the end counts."] explain: "20.05 ≤ 20.05, so it passes." ``` ### Exact area ### Rounded area ### Diagonal ### Review A range, from the last lesson. ## Make: back to the pizzas ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the pizzas: the comparison done exactly, and then a rounded answer for how much more pizza two mediums give." tasks: - hint: ["Large 225π, two mediums 264.5π.", "Subtract, then use π, then round once."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "How many more square centimetres of pizza do two mediums have than one large? Give the answer to the nearest whole number." steps: - ["$\\text{large} = \\pi \\times 15^2 = 225\\pi$", "radius 15"] - ["$\\text{two mediums} = 2 \\times \\pi \\times 11.5^2 = 264.5\\pi$", "radius 11.5"] - ["$264.5\\pi - 225\\pi = 39.5\\pi$", "keep π exact while subtracting"] - ["$39.5\\pi = 124.09\\ldots \\approx 124$", "round once, at the end"] answer: "124" answerLabel: "Extra pizza (cm²)" tolerance: 0.6 feedback: - ["39.5", "That's the number in front of π. Multiply by π."] - ["125", "39.5 × π = 124.09…, not 125."] criteria: - "I kept π exact until the last step." - "I rounded once." - "My answer is a bit over 120." explain: "39.5π ≈ 124 cm² more pizza from the two mediums." - check: type: question q: "Why didn't you need π's digits to decide which is more pizza?" options: ["π was on both sides, so only the other numbers mattered", "π is exactly 3", "π doesn't affect area"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "π isn't 3: it's 3.14159… and never ends.", "π is in the area formula."] explain: "225π against 264.5π: comparing 225 with 264.5 is enough." ``` ### The extra pizza Back to the pizzas. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Why no digits? Pizza sizes here are made up; real menus differ. **Also used in** - **Design and building.** Circle areas and diagonals come out irrational, and the job decides whether to keep π or round. - **Next.** Year 9 Measurement and Algebra, with more formulas to substitute into. ```teacher summary: Students substitute into formulas with π and roots, keep the value exact while they compare, and round once at the end, using a large pizza against two mediums (AC9M9N01, node 4). time: 35 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 9 min goals: - I can substitute real numbers, including π, into a formula. - I can give an exact answer in terms of π. - I can round at the end and say why. struggle: "Squaring the radius, not the diameter. Ask: half of 30 first." before: > Students need Exact or rounded? and the Year 8 area of a circle. Calculators needed. The one idea: keep π exact while you compare; round once at the end. The common mistake is rounding π to 3 and calling it exact (Pia's working). The pizza sizes are made up for the task. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose one large went by width, not area." - "Run: ask students to say the radius before they square it." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the extra pizza in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for π left unmultiplied until the end." - "Modify: before diameter 12, ask what the radius is." stuck: - see: A student squares 30 to get 900π. ask: Is 30 the radius or the diameter? fix: "The diameter: halve it. r = 15, 225π." - see: A student uses π = 3.14 and calls the answer exact. ask: Does π end at 3.14? fix: "No: it's approximate. Use ≈." stretch: How big would a third pizza have to be to beat both? Use areas in π. support: The formula card A = πr² with a worked example in terms of π. leads: > Finishes AC9M9N01. Where it leads: surface area and volume with π, Pythagoras with roots, error and tolerance. exit: q: A circle has diameter 10 cm. What's its exact area? a: 25π cm². explain: > Keep π or a root exact while you work, and round once at the end. If π is on both sides of a comparison, you can compare the other numbers: $225\pi$ against $264.5\pi$. ```
